citation: Ahn (2026) "The 12 Principles of Animation, Reframed for Games" anim.works
label: Industry / Craft
takeaway: Re-frames each classical principle for interactive, interruptible game animation (states can change mid-motion). Design use: animations must stay responsive - cancel cleanly, never lock the player out.

citation: Tian (2020) "Integrating Visual Effects into 2D Platformer Games to Enhance Play Experiences" Northeastern University thesis
label: Thesis Experiment
takeaway: Experimental 2D platformer study: added VFX (trails, impact flashes, ambient particles) measurably enhanced reported play experience. Design use: even simple 2D games gain engagement from layered VFX.

citation: Flayelle, Brevers, King, Maurage, Perales & Billieux (2023) "A Taxonomy of Technology Design Features that Promote Potentially Addictive Online Behaviours" Nature Reviews Psychology
label: Peer-reviewed Review
takeaway: Taxonomy of design features that can undermine user control (variable rewards, endless feeds, social pressures, scarcity). This is the map for where the ethical line sits: engagement mechanics that remove stopping cues are the risky ones.

citation: King, Delfabbro & Griffiths (2010) "The Role of Structural Characteristics in Problem Video Game Playing: A Review" Cyberpsychology
label: Peer-reviewed Review
takeaway: Classic review of structural features (reinforcement schedules, near-misses, social and avatar features) linked to problem play. Design use: the same features that engage can harm at extremes; intensity is the variable.

citation: Saini & Hodgins (2023) "Investigating Gaming Structural Features Associated with Gaming Disorder" J. of Behavioral Addictions
label: Scoping Review
takeaway: Revised taxonomy: social features, narrative/identity and reward/punishment features dominate the problem-play literature; manipulation/control and presentation features less studied. Design use: reward cadence and social obligation need the most ethical care.

citation: Flayelle, Andronicos, King & Billieux (2025) "Understanding the Interplay Between Video Game Design Features and Dysregulated Gaming Patterns" Addictive Behaviors Reports
label: Peer-reviewed Review
takeaway: Argues design features only produce dysregulated play in interaction with player vulnerabilities - calls for interactionist research. Design use: a feature is not inherently predatory; context and audience matter.

citation: Antons, Liebherr, Brand & Brandtner (2023) "From Game Engagement to Craving Responses" Addictive Behaviors Reports
label: Peer-reviewed Study
takeaway: Flow and immersion relate to craving, mediated by gratification and compensation experiences; at-risk gamers show the compensation path. Design use: build gratification (earned satisfaction), not compensation (escape).

citation: Park & Yap (2024) "A Dualistic Approach to Harmonious and Obsessive Passion: The Impact of Game Mechanics on Mobile Gaming Engagement" Electronic Commerce Research
label: Peer-reviewed Study
takeaway: Netnography + dual theory of passion: some mechanics feed harmonious passion (free, integrated play), others obsessive passion (compelled play). Design use: aim mechanics at harmonious passion - mastery and autonomy over obligation.

citation: Hopson / Bungie (2012) "There is No Skinner Box, Says Bungie User Research Lead" Game Developer
label: Industry
takeaway: Bungie's research lead revisits his 2001 'Behavioral Game Design': reward schedules are one tool among many, not a mind-control box; fun and meaning still rule. Design use: use schedules lightly; they cannot rescue a boring game.

citation: Attard (2014) "Liberty Bell, Liberty Bell... Cherry: Gaming, Gambling and the Near-Miss" Game Developer
label: Industry
takeaway: How the near-miss (almost-winning) works as operant conditioning in slots and how game designers adapt it; flags misuse. Design use: showing how close a loss was can motivate, but overuse mimics gambling - ethical line.

citation: Kim (2014) "The Compulsion Loop in Game Design Explained" gamemakers.com
label: Industry
takeaway: Traces the compulsion loop (action -> reward -> new goal) from Hopson 2001 through Zynga-era social games. Design use: a tight core loop is the engine of 'one more go'; keep the loop fair and completable.

citation: Huang (2014) "Moral Game Design" Game Developer
label: Industry / Ethics
takeaway: Practitioner essay: distinguish games that add to players' lives from those that only extract time; designers own that choice. Design use: build the kind of engagement you'd thank a game for.

citation: Billieux, Van der Linden, Achab, Khazaal et al. (2013) "Why Do You Play World of Warcraft?" Computers in Human Behavior
label: Peer-reviewed Study
takeaway: Self-reported motivations (achievement, social, immersion) map onto in-game behaviors; motives predict patterns of involvement. Design use: serve multiple motives so no single compulsive hook carries the game.

citation: The Guardian (2014) "My Favourite Waste of Time: Why Candy Crush and Angry Birds Are So Compulsive"
label: Journalism
takeaway: Reported look at casual-game compulsiveness: simple loops, variable rewards, near-misses and low friction keep players returning. Design use: the strongest casual hooks are simple, fast and endlessly restartable.

citation: Birk, van der Hof & van Rooij (2024) "Behavioral Design in Video Games" ACM
label: Peer-reviewed Framework
takeaway: Proposes adding an ethical-responsible motive to behavioral game design taxonomies, with a visualized taxonomy covering dark patterns and wellbeing. Design use: the closest thing to a published checklist for where engaging becomes exploitative.
